title: Pat Gelsinger Says Intel's Downfall Began When Non-Engineers Took the Wheel
excerpt: The former CEO traces the chipmaker's decline to a finance-first leadership culture that lost touch with engineering discipline, warning of deeper lessons for the global semiconductor race.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Pat Gelsinger attributes Intel's decline to finance-first leadership neglecting engineering discipline.
  • Intel's dismissal of GPU computing was a costly strategic error, allowing Nvidia to thrive.
  • Current CEO Lip-Bu Tan has met initial timelines but Intel still lags behind TSMC.
  • Intel's struggles impact many Indian-origin semiconductor professionals in the US workforce.
  • Gelsinger warns that losing engineering culture poses risks for the entire semiconductor industry.
  • Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger says the chipmaker's decline began when finance-oriented executives replaced engineers at the top, eroding the company's core technical discipline.
  • Gelsinger admits Intel "scoffed" at NVIDIA's GPU bet while riding high on CPU dominance, calling it one of the costliest strategic misreads in tech history.
  • His successor Lip-Bu Tan has delivered Intel's 18A process node on the original five-year timeline, but the company still trails TSMC and faces an uncertain foundry future.
  • Intel's struggles have direct implications for Indian-origin semiconductor professionals, who make up a significant share of the US chip workforce navigating industry upheaval.

The Engineer Who Saw the Rot

Pat Gelsinger joined Intel at 18 and rose to chief technology officer before leaving in 2009 to run VMware. When he returned as CEO in 2021, he expected a turnaround challenge. What he found was worse.

"The decay was deeper and harder than I'd realized," Gelsinger told the Financial Times. In the five years before his return, "not a single product was delivered on schedule." Basic engineering disciplines had collapsed. "It's like, wow, we don't know how to engineer anymore," he said.

Gelsinger traces the rot to a specific inflection point: when Intel's leadership shifted from engineers to finance-first executives who prioritized margins over manufacturing investment. The result was a company that lost its technical edge precisely when the industry was about to be reshaped by artificial intelligence.

![Financial Times — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/8a/Financial_Times_22_February_2021_cover.jpg) > **"Meanwhile, Nvidia bet on purebred GPUs and is now among the world's most valuable companies.

"The decay was deeper and harder than I'd realized."**

The NVIDIA Blind Spot

Perhaps the most damaging admission in Gelsinger's post-mortem is Intel's dismissal of GPU computing. At Nvidia's GTC 2025 conference, Gelsinger conceded that Intel "scoffed" at Jensen Huang's bet on graphics processors while Intel was riding high on CPU dominance.

The company's attempt to build its own GPU, the ill-fated Larrabee project, tried to force the x86 CPU architecture into GPU territory instead of designing a purpose-built chip. It failed. Meanwhile, Nvidia bet on purebred GPUs and is now among the world's most valuable companies.

"The decay was deeper and harder than I'd realized. Not a single product was delivered on schedule. It's like, wow, we don't know how to engineer anymore."

— Pat Gelsinger, former Intel CEO

Intel funded three AI chip projects simultaneously by 2019, including its own GPU effort and two acquisitions. None made significant inroads against Nvidia or AMD. According to Reuters, Gelsinger made ambitious AI-chip revenue projections to clients including Microsoft and Amazon, but when customers sought details, Intel managers had little to show.

The GPU Misstep
›Intel scoffed at Nvidia's GPU strategy.
›Larrabee project failed to compete with Nvidia.
›Nvidia is now among the world's most valuable companies.
›Intel's AI chip projects failed to gain traction.

The TSMC Rift and Foundry Gamble

Gelsinger's turnaround strategy hinged on two bets: catching up to TSMC's manufacturing prowess and transforming Intel into a contract chipmaker for outside companies. Both proved harder than advertised.

His public comments about Taiwan's geopolitical vulnerability — "You don't want all of your eggs in the basket of a Taiwan fab" — alienated TSMC, which reportedly revoked a 40 percent discount on wafer pricing. Intel's stock fell 62 percent during Gelsinger's tenure, the dividend was eliminated, and the company was removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

The board forced him out in December 2024, four years into a five-year plan. Gelsinger concedes he was "very focused on managing down" and should have managed "up" more, including pushing for greater semiconductor expertise on the board itself.

What Comes Next for Intel

Current CEO Lip-Bu Tan has kept Intel in the manufacturing race and delivered the 18A process node within Gelsinger's original timeline. But the company still trails TSMC in advanced chipmaking and has yet to attract major foundry customers beyond small contracts from Amazon and the US military.

The CHIPS Act, which Gelsinger lobbied for more aggressively than any other CEO, has provided Intel with up to $45 billion in US government support. But Gelsinger himself called the implementation "hideous," noting that two and a half years passed before any funds were dispensed.

Gelsinger now predicts quantum computing will eventually displace GPUs, claiming the shift could happen within two years, while Nvidia's Huang puts the timeline at two decades. "We're heading into the most thrilling decade or two for technologists," Gelsinger said.

The Diaspora Dimension

Intel's trajectory matters acutely to the Indian tech diaspora. The company employs thousands of Indian-origin engineers across its design and manufacturing operations, and its struggles have rippled through the broader semiconductor workforce. With more than 150,000 tech layoffs in 2026 and Intel itself cutting over 15,000 jobs, Indian H-1B holders in the chip industry face heightened uncertainty even as companies like TSMC and Samsung expand US operations. Gelsinger's warning about the cost of losing engineering culture resonates beyond Intel — it is a cautionary tale for an industry that the diaspora has helped build.
